tracks.title: Who holds the key
tracks.text: Lesson 09 point 9 — escrow. A sub-lesson, under the VFS… the disk. The bundles lesson ended with a small bombshell. Part of a shipped disk can be ciphertext — a lock the recipient can't open — and the manifest carries only a reference to a key… never the key itself. [curious] Which raises the one question every copy-protection scheme in history has answered badly. Fine — so where is the key… and what stops the wrong person getting it? That's this whole page. The release side of sealing. Where the key actually lives… who decides to release it… and why handing over a key is not a file operation at all. It's a decision.

tracks.title: Who holds the key
tracks.text: First — who holds the key? Every naive answer is a honeypot. Consider three. First, put the key in the file. Now you've shipped the lock taped to its own key — that's theater. Second, put it on a server, in plaintext. Now one breach of that server is every customer's content… all at once. Third, draw a login screen over the data and hope nobody looks underneath. [sarcastic] But the attacker owns the client. Three failure modes… one shared mistake. Treating the key as a thing that lives somewhere… instead of a decision made by someone. The sealing side — how an entry becomes ciphertext — has its own lesson. This page answers the harder question. Once it's locked… who turns the key?

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: The definition. Escrow is the runtime-held content-key store… and its posture-gated release. Plaintext keys never travel with the sealed bytes. A key is handed over only by an access decision, at the engine, against a real identity. A thing a server decides to give you… not a thing you find. The engine's own source calls the store the real dead-man switch. The plaintext key is never written into the bundle — it's escrowed under an identifier, and the bundle carries only a reference. [curious] Pull the key from the store… and every copy of that bundle, everywhere, goes dark at once. That's the switch.

tracks.title: The release path
tracks.text: The release path. Here's the whole flow — happy path and denial in one breath. Picture five players in a row. First, the client, holding a sealed bundle. Second, the auth ladder. Third, the access gate. And fourth, the escrow store itself, sitting in memory. The client reads the locked entry's key identifier, and posts it to the engine — slash rcp slash key — with a bearer token. The auth ladder resolves an identity… a user, a tenant. The gate decides — posture, gated data… demand, data. Now the fork. On allow… the store returns the raw key, base64-encoded, in a small body. Two hundred. On deny… the engine returns the uniform error envelope — code unauthorized, retryable false. Four oh one. And here's the elegant part. A denied key request and a denied page request… are indistinguishable. The same shape. [excited] A refusal leaks nothing — not even what was refused. One more branch. An authenticated caller asking for a key that doesn't exist gets a genuine four oh four… not found. So existence is disclosed only after you've proven who you are. And the gate has teeth — it refuses the anonymous dev fallback outright. A real user, or nothing.

tracks.title: What the store actually is
tracks.text: Next — what the store actually is. No mystery, and deliberately no new database. It's a single named table… in memory… owned by a process that starts itself on the first write. The smallest thing that can hold a key while the runtime is alive. The surface is four verbs. First, put — store a key, overwriting. Second, get — return the key, or no such key. Third, delete — that's revocation, and it's idempotent… deleting twice is harmless. And fourth, the clever one — keyfn. When a bundle is sealed, the seal step asks keyfn for a key per entry. Keyfn mints a fresh thirty-two-byte key, computes an identifier, and escrows the key… all in one motion. So the very act of sealing populates the store. And the identifier is readable on purpose. It's the workbook id, a colon, then the path base64-encoded. A shop sealing its disk produces shop-colon… and if you decode the tail, you literally read back the filename. [chuckles] The prefix is why two different bundles' keys never collide. One honest consequence, stated right here. The table is memory. Keys do not survive a runtime restart. This is a version-one store… not a hardware vault.

tracks.title: One key opens one door
tracks.text: One key opens one door — even if the broker handing it out is buggy, or malicious. And that guarantee doesn't live in the access code. It lives in the cryptography. Picture key A meeting two doors. Door A, whose lock was built with identifier A baked in. And door B, built with identifier B. Key A opens door A — match — plaintext. Key A tries door B… and the labels don't agree… auth failed. When an entry is sealed, its identifier is bound into the authentication tag. So a key minted for one entry simply cannot authenticate against another. The adversarial test proves it. Two sealed entries, a and b. A broken broker returns key A for both. Opening halts — error, b, auth failed — because each identifier rode inside its own lock. [excited] The cryptography double-checks the broker. And every failure collapses to the same answer on purpose. Wrong key… tampered bytes… mismatched label — all of them, auth failed, indistinguishably. It fails closed, it never crashes… and it never tells an attacker which thing was wrong.

tracks.title: Sealing the key itself
tracks.text: Now — sealing the key itself. The store solves custody, but a careful listener notices it's still a central place holding plaintext keys. Breach the runtime's memory… and you have everything. Can we do better? Yes — sealed-box key wrap. Instead of storing the plaintext key, the broker stores the key encrypted to a specific recipient. A throwaway keypair does Diffie-Hellman against the recipient's public key… derives a key-encryption-key… and wraps the content key. Anyone with the recipient's public key can wrap to them. Only the recipient's private key can unwrap. So the runtime stores only wrapped keys — one per recipient — never plaintext. And that's the whole argument. There is no central plaintext honeypot. Breach the broker, and you get ciphertext, plus wrapped keys… which are more ciphertext. Not content. Picture the wrapped key's layout — five parts. First, a five-byte magic, w-b-k-w-one — this is a wrapped key, not a sealed entry. Second, the thirty-two-byte ephemeral public key. Third, the twelve-byte nonce. Fourth, the sixteen-byte tag. And fifth, the wrapped key itself. A deliberate rhyme with the sealed-entry envelope — same grammar… different job. And unwrap fails closed just like seal does — wrong recipient, tamper, wrong label… all unwrap-failed, indistinguishably.

tracks.title: One identity, two curves
tracks.text: One identity… two curves. Sealed-box wrap needs the recipient's encryption key. But a tenant already has an identity — a did-key they sign with, minted from their signing key. And the elegant fact is… the encryption key can be derived from the signing key. So a tenant gets an encryption identity for free… with no extra published key. Walk the path. Start with the did-key string. Decode it — base58, multicodec, expect the ed prefix — and out comes a thirty-two-byte signing key. Apply the public map — a single line of field arithmetic, u equals one plus y, over one minus y, modulo two to the two-fifty-five minus nineteen. Out comes the encryption key — the wrap target. And in parallel, on the recipient's own machine only, their seed clamps down to a private encryption key… for unwrapping locally. The whole thing is pure Elixir bignum math… in about a hundred and fifty lines. No external crypto library. And crucially — the host only ever needs the public map. The recipient derives their private half client-side… so the runtime never sees it. One identity does both jobs — it signs, and now it receives keys. There's a real catch here, though… and it's the best story on the page. It's coming, told straight.

tracks.title: What an attacker gets
tracks.text: What an attacker gets. The question a security-minded listener actually wants — at each foothold, what do they walk away with? Five cases. First, the bundle alone — just ciphertext. The key is not in the file… and a test asserts the manifest never carries a key field. Second, the bundle plus the wire — still ciphertext, assuming transport is encrypted. We assume that layer… and we won't overclaim past it. Third, a breach of the broker in escrow mode — the plaintext keys it currently holds in memory. That's the honeypot the wrap lane removes. Fourth, that same breach in wrapped mode — ciphertext, plus wrapped keys, which are more ciphertext. No content. Nothing plaintext to steal. And fifth, a stolen recipient device — that one recipient's private key, and whatever was wrapped to them… and nothing more. Everyone else is untouched. [excited] And the deny path is tested literally — the refusal response is asserted not to contain the key string anywhere. The bytes provably never appear in a no.

tracks.title: Where escrow ends
tracks.text: Where escrow ends. Four honest limits — stated, not buried. First, the store is in memory. Restart the runtime… and the keys are gone. A version-one store, not a hardware vault. Second — and this is the story we're proudest of — the did-wrapped release lane is built… but deliberately not wired. The wrap machinery and the identity bridge exist and are tested as primitives. The round-trip test passes. But the public map has not been confirmed against a verified reference vector. A candidate was found — three-d-four-oh-one-seven-c-three mapping to e-f-c-six-c-nine-d-zero — but its provenance couldn't be confirmed, the numbers didn't line up, and the test sits in the source marked skip… with the doubts written into the file. So the endpoint stays escrow-only until a verified vector lands. [curious] We refused to trust math we couldn't verify. That restraint… is the feature. Third, the key-derivation is a hash-concat, not the textbook construction, and the gate is binary — authenticated or not, not yet per-key access lists. And fourth — none of this is copy protection. Escrow gates access. A recipient who is legitimately authorized, gets the key, and then leaks the plaintext… is outside what this protects. By design. This is access control over a key… not a claim that an authorized person can be stopped.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Is the key ever in the bundle? No — and it's not a promise, it's a test. The carton carries a reference to a keyring… never a key. What happens when release is denied? You get the uniform error envelope — the same shape any unauthorized call returns — and a test asserts the key bytes are absent from it. A refusal reveals nothing. Can one leaked key unlock everything? No. Every entry gets its own key, and the entry's identifier is bound into its lock — so one key won't open another door. How do I revoke? Delete the key. Idempotent, per-entry… and every copy of that bundle goes dark. Why does the wrapped key have its own magic? So the two lanes can never be confused — a sealed entry and a wrapped key are different things. And why a second curve, if my identity is a signing key? Because signing and encryption use different curve forms… and the runtime derives one from the other. One identity… both jobs.

tracks.title: Back up to the parent
tracks.text: So that's escrow. The release side of sealing. A key is not a thing you find… it's a thing a server decides to give you — against a real identity, where a no looks like every other no. [curious] The way back up is short. This sub-lesson sits under the VFS — the disk that gets sealed in the first place. Its sibling, sealed sections, owns the lock itself — how an entry becomes ciphertext. And bundles is where the references and the envelope were first introduced. Read any of those… and this whole page clicks into place.
